title: The Right Reading Level—or the Right Reading Challenge?
author: Louise Baigelman et al.
summary: This Education Next forum pairs literacy specialist Louise Baigelman, founder of Storyshares, against reading researcher Timothy Shanahan in a debate over his book Leveled Reading, Leveled Lives. Baigelman argues Shanahan's book, despite its title, actually preserves a role for leveled and decodable texts, especially for the large number of older struggling readers who function as 'beginning readers,' and that treating leveled texts and rigor as opposites creates a false choice for real classrooms with wide skill ranges. Shanahan responds that Baigelman conflates 'leveled books' (which everyone agrees have some role) with 'leveled reading' as an instructional regime that caps students' growth by never exposing them to grade-level complexity; he maintains that the research record shows most students learn more when taught with more challenging texts, with true beginning readers as the narrow exception. The exchange surfaces a genuine disagreement over how to interpret NAEP and decoding-threshold research on Gen Z literacy, and over what current teachers are actually doing in classrooms with mixed-level students.
points: Baigelman argues Shanahan's book quietly preserves several exceptions for leveled and decodable texts, for beginning readers, for independent reading, and for supplementing (not replacing) grade-level 'anchor texts.'
She contends leveled and challenging texts should coexist ('both-and,' not 'either-or'), especially given how many older students still lack basic decoding skills.

Shanahan responds that Baigelman conflates 'leveled books' (a value-neutral concept) with 'leveled reading' as an instructional regime that caps growth by permanently limiting struggling students to below-grade-level material.
Both authors draw on the same body of research, NAEP 2024 data and an ETS 'decoding threshold' study, but interpret what it means for older struggling readers very differently.
Shanahan closes by arguing that the purpose of reading instruction is not to give students practice on books they can already read, but to teach them to surmount increasingly challenging texts.
quotes: Did leveled reading cause our current literacy crisis? Or is there still a place for accessible texts in pursuit of rigor for students who are learning to read, especially beyond 3rd grade?
Framing the issue as a choice between rigor and accessibility creates a false dichotomy; effective instruction should offer both.
Leveled texts are meant to extend, enable, and enhance core learning by providing opportunities for access and practice to the students who cannot read grade-level texts independently.
The problem isn’t that this approach doesn’t teach, it’s that it doesn’t teach well enough.
Most kids make greater gains with more-challenging texts, so restricting them to more-elementary books holds them back.
She fails to distinguish leveled books from leveled reading.
No, the purpose is to enable them to read increasingly challenging texts—books the difficulty of which the students need to learn to surmount.
